writer.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
writer.bio: German philosopher, 1788 to 1860. He held that life is mostly want and suffering and that the wise move is to expect less. Ignored for most of his life, he lived alone in Frankfurt with his poodles and became famous in his sixties.

works.title: The Wisdom of Life
works.note: From Parerga and Paralipomena, 1851, the book of essays that finally made him famous at 63 after thirty years of being ignored.

works.title: Counsels and Maxims
works.note: The second half of his Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, 1851: rules for dealing with yourself, with other people and with fate.

works.title: Studies in Pessimism
works.note: Essays from Parerga and Paralipomena, 1851, on suffering, the emptiness of existence and thinking for yourself.

works.title: On Human Nature
works.note: Essays on character, ethics and free will, taken from Parerga and Paralipomena, 1851.

works.title: The Art of Literature
works.note: Essays on writing, style, reading and thinking for yourself, from Parerga and Paralipomena, 1851.

works.title: Religion: A Dialogue, Etc.
works.note: A dialogue and short essays from Parerga and Paralipomena, 1851.

works.title: The Art of Controversy, Etc.
works.note: Found in his papers after his death. Written around 1830, it lists the tricks people use to win an argument when they are wrong.

quotes.text: In general, indeed, the wise in all ages have always said the same thing, and the fools, who at all times form the immense majority, have in their way too acted alike, and done just the opposite; and so it will continue.
quotes.plain: Everyone knows what is wise. Almost nobody does it.

quotes.text: The world in which a man lives shapes itself chiefly by the way in which he looks at it, and so it proves different to different men; to one it is barren, dull, and superficial; to another rich, interesting, and full of meaning.
quotes.plain: How you see the world decides what it is to you.

quotes.text: In plain language, every man is pent up within the limits of his own consciousness, and cannot directly get beyond those limits any more than he can get beyond his own skin; so external aid is not of much use to him.
quotes.plain: You live inside your own head, and nobody can fix that from outside.

quotes.text: All the pride and pleasure of the world, mirrored in the dull consciousness of a fool, are poor indeed compared with the imagination of Cervantes writing his Don Quixote in a miserable prison.
quotes.plain: A great mind in a cell beats a fool with everything.

quotes.text: Health outweighs all other blessings so much that one may really say that a healthy beggar is happier than an ailing king.
quotes.plain: Health beats status, money and everything else.

quotes.text: An intellectual man in complete solitude has excellent entertainment in his own thoughts and fancies, while no amount of diversity or social pleasure, theatres, excursions and amusements, can ward off boredom from a dullard.
quotes.plain: A full mind is never bored alone. An empty one is bored in a crowd.

quotes.text: A good, temperate, gentle character can be happy in needy circumstances, whilst a covetous, envious and malicious man, even if he be the richest in the world, goes miserable.
quotes.plain: Character makes you happy broke. Greed makes you miserable rich.

quotes.text: The man who is cheerful and merry has always a good reason for being so, the fact, namely, that he is so.
quotes.plain: Being cheerful is its own reason.

quotes.text: So if cheerfulness knocks at our door, we should throw it wide open, for it never comes inopportunely; instead of that, we often make scruples about letting it in.
quotes.plain: Let joy in when it shows up. Do not wait for permission.

quotes.text: Even trees must be shaken by the wind, if they are to thrive.
quotes.plain: You need resistance to grow.

quotes.text: It is not what things are objectively and in themselves, but what they are for us, in our way of looking at them, that makes us happy or the reverse.
quotes.plain: It is not the event that hurts you, it is how you look at it.

quotes.text: It follows from all this that the greatest of follies is to sacrifice health for any other kind of happiness, whatever it may be, for gain, advancement, learning or fame, let alone, then, for fleeting sensual pleasures.
quotes.plain: Never trade your health for money, fame or fun.

quotes.text: The most general survey shows us that the two foes of human happiness are pain and boredom.
quotes.plain: Life swings between pain and boredom.

quotes.text: Nothing is so good a protection against such misery as inward wealth, the wealth of the mind, because the greater it grows, the less room it leaves for boredom.
quotes.plain: Build your mind and boredom has nowhere to live.

quotes.text: True, if quality of intellect could be made up for by quantity, it might be worth while to live even in the great world; but unfortunately, a hundred fools together will not make one wise man.
quotes.plain: Crowds do not add up to wisdom.

quotes.text: Ordinary people think merely how they shall spend their time; a man of any talent tries to use it.
quotes.plain: Ordinary people kill time. Talented people use it.

quotes.text: Because people have no thoughts to deal in, they deal cards, and try and win one another's money.
quotes.plain: People with nothing in their heads fill the hours with games.

quotes.text: What one human being can be to another is not a very great deal: in the end every one stands alone, and the important thing is who it is that stands alone.
quotes.plain: In the end you stand alone, so what matters is who you are.

quotes.text: There is not much to be got anywhere in the world. It is filled with misery and pain; and if a man escapes these, boredom lies in wait for him at every corner.
quotes.plain: The world hands you pain, and if not pain then boredom.

quotes.text: Nay more; it is evil which generally has the upper hand, and folly makes the most noise.
quotes.plain: Evil usually wins and fools are loud. Do not take either as proof of anything.

quotes.text: In such a world as this, a man who is rich in himself is like a bright, warm, happy room at Christmastide, while without are the frost and snow of a December night.
quotes.plain: If you are rich inside, the cold outside does not reach you.

quotes.text: It is a great piece of folly to sacrifice the inner for the outer man, to give the whole or the greater part of one's quiet, leisure and independence for splendor, rank, pomp, titles and honor.
quotes.plain: Do not sell your peace and independence for status.

quotes.text: Card-playing is, in fact, a mere tickling of the will.
quotes.plain: Games are cheap stimulation for a bored mind.

quotes.text: The ordinary life of every day, so far as it is not moved by passion, is tedious and insipid; and if it is so moved, it soon becomes painful.
quotes.plain: Ordinary life is dull until passion shows up, then it hurts.

quotes.text: The ordinary man places his life's happiness in things external to him, in property, rank, wife and children, friends, society, and the like, so that when he loses them or finds them disappointing, the foundation of his happiness is destroyed.
quotes.plain: Put your happiness in outside things and they can wreck it.

quotes.text: The man of inner wealth wants nothing from outside but the negative gift of undisturbed leisure, to develop and mature his intellectual faculties, that is, to enjoy his wealth; in short, he wants permission to be himself, his whole life long, every day and every hour.
quotes.plain: What you need is room to be yourself.

quotes.text: In much wisdom is much grief; and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow.
quotes.plain: The more you know, the more it hurts.

quotes.text: The great affliction of all philistines is that they have no interest in ideas, and that, to escape being bored, they are in constant need of realities.
quotes.plain: Shallow people need constant action because ideas bore them.

quotes.text: A man never feels the loss of things which it never occurs to him to ask for; he is just as happy without them; whilst another, who may have a hundred times as much, feels miserable because he has not got the one thing he wants.
quotes.plain: You are only as poor as the things you want and lack.

quotes.text: Riches, one may say, are like sea-water; the more you drink the thirstier you become; and the same is true of fame.
quotes.plain: Wealth and fame make you thirstier, not satisfied.

quotes.text: Discontent springs from a constant endeavor to increase the amount of our claims, when we are powerless to increase the amount which will satisfy them.
quotes.plain: You get unhappy when your wants grow faster than your means.

quotes.text: Money alone is absolutely good, because it is not only a concrete satisfaction of one need in particular; it is an abstract satisfaction of all.
quotes.plain: Money is the one good that stands in for every other.

quotes.text: Countless numbers of people find themselves in want, simply because, when they had money, they spent it only to get momentary relief from the feeling of boredom which oppressed them.
quotes.plain: People go broke spending to escape boredom.

quotes.text: If you stroke a cat, it will purr; and, as inevitably, if you praise a man, a sweet expression of delight will appear on his face; and even though the praise is a palpable lie, it will be welcome, if the matter is one on which he prides himself.
quotes.plain: Flattery works on everyone, even when it is false.

quotes.text: And if ever we have had an opportunity of seeing how the greatest of men will meet with nothing but slight from half-a-dozen blockheads, we shall understand that to lay great value upon what other people say is to pay them too much honor.
quotes.plain: Even great people get dismissed by fools. Their opinion is not worth your weight.

quotes.text: It is solicitude about what others will say that underlies all our vanity and pretension, yes, and all our show and swagger too.
quotes.plain: Most vanity and show is fear of what people will say.

quotes.text: It is observable that a retired mode of life has an exceedingly beneficial influence on our peace of mind, and this is mainly because we thus escape having to live constantly in the sight of others, and pay everlasting regard to their casual opinions; in a word, we are able to return upon ourselves.
quotes.plain: Less time in other people's eyes means more peace.

quotes.text: Pride works from within; it is the direct appreciation of oneself. Vanity is the desire to arrive at this appreciation indirectly, from without.
quotes.plain: Pride comes from inside. Vanity begs for it from outside.

quotes.text: No doubt, when modesty was made a virtue, it was a very advantageous thing for the fools; for everybody is expected to speak of himself as if he were one.
quotes.plain: Modesty is a gift to fools, who then pretend to be equals.

quotes.text: The cheapest sort of pride is national pride; for if a man is proud of his own nation, it argues that he has no qualities of his own of which he can be proud; otherwise he would not have recourse to those which he shares with so many millions of his fellowmen.
quotes.plain: Being proud of what millions share means you have nothing of your own.

quotes.text: Every nation mocks at other nations, and all are right.
quotes.plain: Everybody is a fool to somebody, and they are right.

quotes.text: The man who breaks confidence has for ever forfeited confidence, whatever he may do, and whoever he may be; and the bitter consequences of the loss of confidence can never be averted.
quotes.plain: Break trust once and you are done.

quotes.text: Do you think, said Socrates, that if an ass happened to kick me, I should resent it?
quotes.plain: Socrates would not resent a kick from a donkey, so why resent a fool?

quotes.text: A man must himself have but a poor opinion of his own worth who hastens to prevent the utterance of an unfavorable opinion by giving his enemy a black eye.
quotes.plain: Hitting back shows you doubt your own worth.

quotes.text: True appreciation of his own value will make a man really indifferent to insult; but if he cannot help resenting it, a little shrewdness and culture will enable him to save appearances and dissemble his anger.
quotes.plain: If you know your worth, insults slide off.

quotes.text: Fame is the undying brother of ephemeral honor.
quotes.plain: Fame outlives honor.

quotes.text: Everyone can make a claim to honor; very few to fame, as being attainable only in virtue of extraordinary achievements.
quotes.plain: Anyone can have honor. Fame takes extraordinary work.

quotes.text: The influence of an action, be it never so noble, can last but a short time; but a work of genius is a living influence, beneficial and ennobling throughout the ages.
quotes.plain: Deeds fade. Great work keeps working for centuries.

quotes.text: Of Alexander the Great we have but the name and the record; but Plato and Aristotle, Homer and Horace are alive, and as directly at work to-day as they were in their own lifetime.
quotes.plain: Alexander is a name. Plato and Homer are still at work.

quotes.text: That was an incomparable fine saying of Seneca's, that fame follows merit as surely as the body casts a shadow; sometimes falling in front, and sometimes behind.
quotes.plain: Merit gets recognized, sometimes late.

quotes.text: As a general rule, the longer a man's fame is likely to last, the later it will be in coming; for all excellent products require time for their development.
quotes.plain: The longer the fame will last, the later it arrives.

quotes.text: The fame which lasts to posterity is like an oak, of very slow growth; and that which endures but a little while, like plants which spring up in a year and then die; whilst false fame is like a fungus, shooting up in a night and perishing as soon.
quotes.plain: Lasting fame grows like an oak. Fake fame pops up like a mushroom and dies.

quotes.text: People are more likely to appreciate the man who serves the circumstances of his own brief hour, or the temper of the moment, belonging to it, living and dying with it.
quotes.plain: Easy to love the man of the moment. He dies with the moment.

quotes.text: There is but one thing to be done, though how difficult! the foolish must become wise, and that they can never be.
quotes.plain: The only fix for fools is wisdom, and they never get it.

quotes.text: The man who seeks to do what is good and genuine, must avoid what is bad, and be ready to defy the opinions of the mob, nay, even to despise it and its misleaders.
quotes.plain: Do good work, and be ready to ignore the crowd.

quotes.text: The truth is that fame means nothing but what a man is in comparison with others.
quotes.plain: Fame is only comparison.

quotes.text: Not fame, but that which deserves to be famous, is what a man should hold in esteem.
quotes.plain: Respect what deserves fame, not the fame itself.

quotes.text: It would be a miserable existence which should make its value or want of value depend upon what other people think; but such would be the life of a hero or a genius if its worth consisted in fame, that is, in the applause of the world.
quotes.plain: If your worth depends on other people, your life is miserable.

quotes.text: He who deserves fame without getting it possesses by far the more important element of happiness, which should console him for the loss of the other.
quotes.plain: If you earned it but did not get it, you still hold what matters.

quotes.text: If admiration were his chief aim, there would be nothing in him to admire.
quotes.plain: If you only want admiration, there is nothing in you to admire.

quotes.text: The truest fame, the fame that comes after death, is never heard of by its recipient; and yet he is called a happy man.
quotes.plain: The best fame arrives after you are gone, and you are happy anyway.

quotes.text: It is only work done from the heart that ever gains the laurel.
quotes.plain: Only work you mean ever wins anything.

quotes.text: The value of posthumous fame lies in deserving it; and this is its own reward.
quotes.plain: Deserving it is the reward.

quotes.text: People are always swayed by authority; and where fame is widespread, it means that ninety-nine out of a hundred take it on faith alone.
quotes.plain: Most fame is people repeating what they were told.

quotes.text: Would a musician feel flattered by the loud applause of an audience if he knew that they were nearly all deaf, and that, to conceal their infirmity, they set to work to clap vigorously as soon as ever they saw one or two persons applauding?
quotes.plain: Applause means nothing if the crowd cannot tell good from bad.

quotes.text: Life is such a poor business that the strictest economy must be exercised in its good things.
quotes.plain: Life is thin, so spend its good things carefully.

quotes.text: There is no greater consolation in age than the feeling of having put the whole force of one's youth into works which still remain young.
quotes.plain: Put your whole youth into work that stays young.

quotes.text: There is no doubt that life is given us, not to be enjoyed, but to be overcome, to be got over.
quotes.plain: Life is something you get through, not something you collect pleasures from.

quotes.text: To desire to get rid of an evil is a definite object, but to desire a better fortune than one has is blind folly.
quotes.plain: Fix a real problem. Chasing a vague better life just keeps you restless.

quotes.text: It is prudent and wise, I say, to reduce one's claims, if only for the reason that it is extremely easy to be very unhappy; while to be very happy is not indeed difficult, but quite impossible.
quotes.plain: Expect less and you get hurt less. Constant bliss was never on the menu.

quotes.text: Joy is like the gold in the Australian mines, found only now and then, as it were, by the caprice of chance, and according to no rule or law; oftenest in very little grains, and very seldom in heaps.
quotes.plain: Joy shows up in small grains at random moments, not on schedule at the big events.

quotes.text: Everything in the world is like a hollow nut; there is little kernel anywhere, and when it does exist, it is still more rare to find it in the shell.
quotes.plain: Most shiny things are empty inside. The real stuff is rare and hides.

quotes.text: To be irritated by trifles, a man must be well off; for in misfortunes trifles are unfelt.
quotes.plain: If small stuff bugs you, your life is going fine. Real trouble makes trifles disappear.

quotes.text: To make extensive preparations for life, no matter what form they may take, is one of the greatest and commonest of follies.
quotes.plain: Stop preparing to live. Start doing the thing now.

quotes.text: Instead of finding, as we expected, pleasure, happiness, joy, we get experience, insight, knowledge, a real and permanent blessing, instead of a fleeting and illusory one.
quotes.plain: You chase happiness and end up with wisdom, which lasts longer.

quotes.text: In their search for gold, the alchemists discovered other things, gunpowder, china, medicines, the laws of nature. There is a sense in which we are all alchemists.
quotes.plain: The goal you chase may fail, but what you find on the way can be worth more.

quotes.text: Distance, which makes objects look small to the outward eye, makes them look big to the eye of thought. The present alone is true and actual; it is the only time which possesses full reality, and our existence lies in it exclusively.
quotes.plain: Past and future loom bigger in your head than they are. Only now is real.

quotes.text: It is the height of folly to refuse the present hour of happiness, or wantonly to spoil it by vexation at by-gones or uneasiness about what is to come.
quotes.plain: Don't ruin a good hour by stewing over the past or the future.

quotes.text: We should always collect that To-day comes only once, and never returns. We fancy that it will come again to-morrow; but To-morrow is another day, which, in its turn, comes once only.
quotes.plain: Today does not repeat. Tomorrow is a different day, not a refund.

quotes.text: A thousand gay and pleasant hours are wasted in ill-humor; we let them slip by unenjoyed, and sigh for them in vain when the sky is overcast.
quotes.plain: You will miss these good hours later. Notice them now.

quotes.text: Limitations always make for happiness.
quotes.plain: Fewer options, fewer worries. Narrow focus is peaceful.

quotes.text: Experience of the world may be looked upon as a kind of text, to which reflection and knowledge form the commentary.
quotes.plain: Living teaches nothing unless you stop and think about it.

quotes.text: A man can be himself only so long as he is alone; and if he does not love solitude, he will not love freedom; for it is only when he is alone that he is really free.
quotes.plain: You only get to be yourself when no one is watching. Learn to like your own company.

quotes.text: The young should early be trained to bear being left alone; for it is a source of happiness and peace of mind.
quotes.plain: Learn to be alone while you're young. It pays off for life.

quotes.text: The more a man has in himself, the less others can be to him.
quotes.plain: The richer your inner life, the less you need the crowd.

quotes.text: Ordinary people are sociable and complaisant just from the very opposite feeling; to bear others' company is easier for them than to bear their own.
quotes.plain: Many people are around others because they can't stand being alone with themselves.

quotes.text: It is the monotony of his own nature that makes a man find solitude intolerable.
quotes.plain: If being alone feels unbearable, it's because there's not much going on inside yet.

quotes.text: Peace of mind is impossible without a considerable amount of solitude.
quotes.plain: You need hours alone to be calm. No way around it.

quotes.text: To be soon on friendly, or even affectionate, terms with solitude is like winning a gold mine; but this is not something which everybody can do.
quotes.plain: Being comfortable alone is a rare, valuable skill.

quotes.text: To be alone is the fate of all great minds, a fate deplored at times, but still always chosen as the less grievous of two evils.
quotes.plain: Anyone doing something great ends up alone sometimes. It's the cheaper cost.

quotes.text: Society is in this respect like a fire, the wise man warming himself at a proper distance from it; not coming too close, like the fool, who, on getting scorched, runs away and shivers in solitude, loud in his complaint that the fire burns.
quotes.plain: Enjoy people from a safe distance. Don't get burned and then blame the fire.

quotes.text: Envy is natural to man; and still, it is at once a vice and a source of misery.
quotes.plain: Envy feels normal and it only hurts you.

quotes.text: See well to your girths, and then ride on boldly.
quotes.plain: Prepare properly, then commit and stop second guessing.

quotes.text: If we have made obvious mistakes, we should not try, as we generally do, to gloss them over, or to find something to excuse or extenuate them; we should admit to ourselves that we have committed faults, and open our eyes wide to all their enormity, in order that we may firmly resolve to avoid them in time to come.
quotes.plain: Own your mistakes fully, no excuses, so you don't repeat them.

quotes.text: We should give no play to imagination here; for imagination is not judgment, it only conjures up visions, inducing an unprofitable and often very painful mood.
quotes.plain: Your imagination invents scary stories. That's not the same as thinking.

quotes.text: Night gives a black look to everything, whatever it may be.
quotes.plain: Everything looks worse at night. Wait for morning before you judge.

quotes.text: Do not shorten the morning by getting up late, or waste it in unworthy occupations or in talk; look upon it as the quintessence of life, as to a certain extent sacred.
quotes.plain: Protect your mornings. They're your best hours.

quotes.text: Each day is a little life: every waking and rising a little birth, every fresh morning a little youth, every going to rest and sleep a little death.
quotes.plain: Every day is a full small life. Treat it that way.

quotes.text: The smallest annoyance, whether it comes from our fellow-men or from the things around us, may swell up into a monster of dreadful aspect, putting us at our wits' end, and all because we go on brooding over our troubles and painting them in the most glaring colors and on the largest scale.
quotes.plain: Brooding blows small irritations up into monsters.

quotes.text: It is much better to take a very calm and prosaic view of what is disagreeable; for that is the easiest way of bearing it.
quotes.plain: Look at the bad thing flatly, without drama. It hurts less.

quotes.text: If you hold small objects close to your eyes, you limit your field of vision and shut out the world.
quotes.plain: Small problems held too close block out everything else.

quotes.text: It is a source of consolation to look back upon those great misfortunes which never happened.
quotes.plain: Most of the disasters you feared never came. Remember that.

quotes.text: Our thoughts must be arranged, as it were, in little drawers, so that we may open one without disturbing any of the others.
quotes.plain: Handle one problem at a time. Close the others.

quotes.text: Nothing will protect us from external compulsion so much as the control of ourselves; and, as Seneca says, to submit yourself to reason is the way to make everything else submit to you, si tibi vis omnia subjicere, te subjice rationi.
quotes.plain: Rule yourself or the world will rule you.

quotes.text: There is a direct pleasure in seeing work grow under one's hands day by day, until at last it is finished.
quotes.plain: Watching something you build grow daily is its own reward.

quotes.text: Let everyone, then, do something, according to the measure of his capacities. To have no regular work, no set sphere of activity, what a miserable thing it is!
quotes.plain: Having no work to do is misery. Get something to build.

quotes.text: Effort, struggles with difficulties! that is as natural to a man as grubbing in the ground is to a mole.
quotes.plain: Struggle is your natural habitat, not a defect.

quotes.text: To overcome difficulties is to experience the full delight of existence, no matter where the obstacles are encountered; whether in the affairs of life, in commerce or business; or in mental effort, the spirit of inquiry that tries to master its subject.
quotes.plain: The joy of life is in beating obstacles.

quotes.text: There is always something pleasurable in the struggle and the victory.
quotes.plain: The fight itself and the win are both satisfying.

quotes.text: A man should avoid being led on by the phantoms of his imagination.
quotes.plain: Don't steer your life by daydreams of how it will feel.

quotes.text: The way to harden the body is to impose a great deal of labor and effort upon it in the days of good health, to exercise it, both as a whole and in its several parts, and to habituate it to withstand all kinds of noxious influences.
quotes.plain: Train hard while healthy so the body can take hits later.

quotes.text: It is most important to allow the brain the full measure of sleep which is required to restore it; for sleep is to a man's whole nature what winding up is to a clock.
quotes.plain: Sleep is what winds you back up. Don't skimp.

quotes.text: The brain can be ruined by overstrain, just like the eyes.
quotes.plain: Overworking your mind breaks it like any other muscle.

quotes.text: In making his way through life, a man will find it useful to be ready and able to do two things: to look ahead and to overlook: the one will protect him from loss and injury, the other from disputes and squabbles.
quotes.plain: Plan ahead, and let petty stuff slide.

quotes.text: To become indignant at their conduct is as foolish as to be angry with a stone because it rolls into your path.
quotes.plain: People act per their nature. Raging at them is like raging at a rock.

quotes.text: Great minds are like eagles, and build their nest in some lofty solitude.
quotes.plain: Great people live apart from the crowd.

quotes.text: No man can see over his own height.
quotes.plain: You can only recognize in others what you already have in you.

quotes.text: Intellect is invisible to the man who has none.
quotes.plain: Some people can't see your quality. Don't take it personally.

quotes.text: Most men are so thoroughly subjective that nothing really interests them but themselves.
quotes.plain: People are mostly thinking about themselves, not you.

quotes.text: He who can see truly in the midst of general infatuation is like a man whose watch keeps good time, when all clocks in the town in which he lives are wrong.
quotes.plain: Being right when everyone's wrong is lonely. Keep your time anyway.

quotes.text: Men are like children, in that, if you spoil them, they become naughty.
quotes.plain: Too much indulgence makes people entitled.

quotes.text: The only way to attain superiority in dealing with men, is to let it be seen that you are independent of them.
quotes.plain: Needing nobody gives you the upper hand.

quotes.text: A man shows his character just in the way in which he deals with trifles, for then he is off his guard.
quotes.plain: Watch how someone handles small things. That's who they are.

quotes.text: There is nothing, absolutely nothing, that a man cannot forget, but not himself, his own character.
quotes.plain: You can forget anything except who you are.

quotes.text: In savage countries they eat one another, in civilized they deceive one another; and that is what people call the way of the world!
quotes.plain: We swapped violence for lying and called it civilization.

quotes.text: To affect a quality, and to plume yourself upon it, is just to confess that you have not got it.
quotes.plain: Bragging about a trait shows you lack it.

quotes.text: He who criticises others, works at the reformation of himself.
quotes.plain: Judging others sharpens your own standards.

quotes.text: We require a looking-glass for the due dressing of our morals.
quotes.plain: Other people's flaws show you your own.

quotes.text: Your friends will tell you that they are sincere; your enemies are really so.
quotes.plain: Friends flatter you. Enemies tell you the truth.

quotes.text: A friend in need, as the saying goes, is rare. Nay, it is just the contrary; no sooner have you made a friend than he is in need, and asks for a loan.
quotes.plain: Everyone's a friend until they need something.

quotes.text: A man must be still a greenhorn in the ways of the world, if he imagines that he can make himself popular in society by exhibiting intelligence and discernment.
quotes.plain: Showing off how smart you are does not make people like you.

quotes.text: To show your intelligence and discernment is only an indirect way of reproaching other people for being dull and incapable.
quotes.plain: Flexing your brains makes others feel stupid, so they resent you.

quotes.text: To combine politeness with pride is a masterpiece of wisdom.
quotes.plain: Be courteous and still keep your self-respect.

quotes.text: Never combat any man's opinion; for though you reached the age of Methuselah, you would never have done setting him right upon all the absurd things that he believes.
quotes.plain: You can't correct everyone. Save your energy.

quotes.text: If you want your judgment to be accepted, express it coolly and without passion.
quotes.plain: Say it calmly if you want to be believed.

quotes.text: Even when you are fully justified in praising yourself, you should never be seduced into doing so.
quotes.plain: Let your work speak. Self-praise backfires.

quotes.text: Prudence exacts that a wide gulf should be fixed between what we think and what we say.
quotes.plain: Keep a gap between your thoughts and your mouth.

quotes.text: Do not tell a friend anything that you would conceal from an enemy.
quotes.plain: Keep real secrets to yourself.

quotes.text: A secret is in my custody, if I keep it; but should it escape me, it is I who am the prisoner.
quotes.plain: Once a secret leaves your mouth, it owns you.

quotes.text: The tree of silence bears the fruit of peace.
quotes.plain: Staying quiet keeps you calm.

quotes.text: Money is never spent to so much advantage as when you have been cheated out of it; for at one stroke you have purchased prudence.
quotes.plain: Getting scammed is tuition. At least learn something.

quotes.text: Give way neither to love nor to hate, is one-half of worldly wisdom: say nothing and believe nothing, the other half.
quotes.plain: Don't be ruled by love or hate, and don't take people at their word.

quotes.text: Anger and hatred should never be shown otherwise than in what you do; and feelings will be all the more effective in action, in so far as you avoid the exhibition of them in any other way. It is only cold-blooded animals whose bite is poisonous.
quotes.plain: Don't shout your anger. Channel it into action.

quotes.text: Our brains are not the wisest part of us.
quotes.plain: Your gut often knows before your head can explain it.

quotes.text: There is no more thriftless proceeding than to try and mend the measured pace of Time. Be careful, then, not to become its debtor.
quotes.plain: Rushing what needs time costs you more later than waiting would.

quotes.text: The most terrible misfortunes are also the most improbable and remote, the least likely to occur.
quotes.plain: The disasters you dread most are the ones least likely to happen.

quotes.text: Whatever fate befalls you, do not give way to great rejoicings or great lamentations; partly because all things are full of change, and your fortune may turn at any moment; partly because men are so apt to be deceived in their judgment as to what is good or bad for them.
quotes.plain: Do not get too high or too low. Things turn, and you cannot tell what is really good for you.

quotes.text: It should never be forgotten that misfortune, be it great or small, is the element in which we live.
quotes.plain: Trouble is the normal state of life, so stop being shocked by it.

quotes.text: What people commonly call Fate is, as a general rule, nothing but their own stupid and foolish conduct.
quotes.plain: Most of what people blame on fate is their own bad choices.

quotes.text: It is not ferocity but cunning that strikes fear into the heart and forebodes danger; so true it is that the human brain is a more terrible weapon than the lion's paw.
quotes.plain: The sharp mind is more dangerous than brute force.

quotes.text: The most finished man of the world would be one who was never irresolute and never in a hurry.
quotes.plain: Be decisive, and never be rushed.

quotes.text: It is a cowardly soul that shrinks or grows faint and despondent as soon as the storm begins to gather, or even when the first cloud appears on the horizon.
quotes.plain: Do not fold at the first sign of trouble.

quotes.text: Our whole life itself, let alone its blessings, would not be worth such a cowardly trembling and shrinking of the heart.
quotes.plain: A life spent cringing is not worth having. Face it.

quotes.text: I may be allowed to express the matter, briefly, thus: the world is glorious to look at, but dreadful in reality.
quotes.plain: Life looks beautiful from outside and is hard from inside.

quotes.text: It would be a great advantage to a young man if his early training could eradicate the idea that the world has a great deal to offer him.
quotes.plain: Expecting the world to hand you things sets you up for disappointment.

quotes.text: If the chief feature of the earlier half of life is a never-satisfied longing after happiness, the later half is characterized by the dread of misfortune.
quotes.plain: First you chase happiness, then you just try to avoid pain.

quotes.text: The chief result gained by experience of life is clearness of view.
quotes.plain: What experience really buys you is seeing things as they are.

quotes.text: In our early days we fancy that the leading events in our life, and the persons who are going to play an important part in it, will make their entrance to the sound of drums and trumpets; but when, in old age, we look back, we find that they all came in quite quietly, slipped in, as it were, by the side-door, almost unnoticed.
quotes.plain: The big turns in life arrive quietly. Notice them.

quotes.text: The wrong side is not so pretty as the right, but it is more instructive; it shows the way in which the threads have been worked together.
quotes.plain: The messy side of life teaches more than the pretty side.

quotes.text: The cheerfulness and vivacity of youth are partly due to the fact that, when we are ascending the hill of life, death is not visible: it lies down at the bottom of the other side.
quotes.plain: Youth feels free because death is out of sight. It is still there.

quotes.text: As long as we are young, people may tell us what they please! we look upon life as endless and use our time recklessly; but the older we become, the more we practice economy.
quotes.plain: Treat your time like it is limited now, not later.

quotes.text: To see how short life is, a man must have grown old, that is to say, he must have lived long.
quotes.plain: You only feel how short life is once a lot of it is gone, so act now.

quotes.text: We cram the years so full of projects that if we were to try and carry them all out, death would come prematurely though we reached the age of Methuselah.
quotes.plain: You plan more than a lifetime can hold. Pick what matters.

quotes.text: Sometimes we credit ourselves with a longing to be in some distant spot, whereas, in truth, we are only longing to have the time back again which we spent there, days when we were younger and fresher than we are now.
quotes.plain: You often miss a time, not a place.

quotes.text: Every generation, no matter how paltry its character, thinks itself much wiser than the one immediately preceding it, let alone those that are more remote.
quotes.plain: Every era thinks it knows better than the last. Stay humble.

quotes.text: Towards the close of life, much the same thing happens as at the end of a bal masqué, the masks are taken off. Then you can see who the people really are, with whom you have come into contact in your passage through the world.
quotes.plain: Time reveals who people really are.

quotes.text: The progress of life shows a man the stuff of which he is made.
quotes.plain: Years of living show you what you are made of.

quotes.text: While the young man fancies that there is a vast amount of good things in the world, if he could only come at them, the old man is steeped in the truth of the Preacher's words, that all things are vanity, knowing that, however gilded the shell, the nut is hollow.
quotes.plain: What you chase looks better from far away than it is.

quotes.text: To be poor when one is old, is a great misfortune.
quotes.plain: Build your money now so your later years are not a struggle.

quotes.text: Death is the great reservoir of Life. Everything comes from Orcus; everything that is alive now was once there. Could we but understand the great trick by which that is done, all would be clear!
quotes.plain: Life comes out of death and goes back to it. It is one cycle.

quotes.text: Each separate misfortune, as it comes, seems, no doubt, to be something exceptional; but misfortune in general is the rule.
quotes.location: On the Sufferings of the World
quotes.plain: Your bad luck feels special but it is normal for everyone.

quotes.text: We are like lambs in a field, disporting themselves under the eye of the butcher, who chooses out first one and then another for his prey.
quotes.location: On the Sufferings of the World
quotes.plain: Good days hide how fragile things are. Do not get comfortable.

quotes.text: No little part of the torment of existence lies in this, that Time is continually pressing upon us, never letting us take breath, but always coming after us, like a taskmaster with a whip.
quotes.location: On the Sufferings of the World
quotes.plain: Time never stops chasing you. That pressure is part of life.

quotes.text: A ship without ballast is unstable and will not go straight.
quotes.location: On the Sufferings of the World
quotes.plain: Some weight and difficulty keeps you steady.

quotes.text: It is a blessing that we do not know what is really going to happen.
quotes.location: On the Sufferings of the World
quotes.plain: Not knowing the future is a mercy. Keep going.

quotes.text: Life is a task to be done. It is a fine thing to say defunctus est; it means that the man has done his task.
quotes.location: On the Sufferings of the World
quotes.plain: Life is work, and the best thing to say at the end is that you finished it.

quotes.text: Of a truth, need and boredom are the two poles of human life.
quotes.location: On the Sufferings of the World
quotes.plain: You are either struggling for something or bored. Both are normal.

quotes.text: If he has a soul above the common, or if he is a man of genius, he will occasionally feel like some noble prisoner of state, condemned to work in the galleys with common criminals; and he will follow his example and try to isolate himself.
quotes.location: On the Sufferings of the World
quotes.plain: If you are above the crowd you will feel out of place and want to be alone.

quotes.text: Pardon's the word to all! Whatever folly men commit, be their shortcomings or their vices what they may, let us exercise forbearance; remembering that when these faults appear in others, it is our follies and vices that we behold.
quotes.location: On the Sufferings of the World
quotes.plain: Go easy on people. Their faults are yours too.

quotes.text: A man finds himself, to his great astonishment, suddenly existing, after thousands and thousands of years of non-existence: he lives for a little while; and then, again, comes an equally long period when he must exist no more.
quotes.plain: You get a short window between two long absences. Use it.

quotes.text: Of every event in our life we can say only for one moment that it is; for ever after, that it was. Every evening we are poorer by a day.
quotes.plain: Each day you spend is gone for good.

quotes.text: We are like a man running downhill, who cannot keep on his legs unless he runs on, and will inevitably fall if he stops; or, again, like a pole balanced on the tip of one's finger; or like a planet, which would fall into its sun the moment it ceased to hurry forward on its way.
quotes.plain: You stay up by moving. Stopping is how you fall.

quotes.text: Unrest is the mark of existence.
quotes.plain: Restlessness is just what being alive is.

quotes.text: In the first place, a man never is happy, but spends his whole life in striving after something which he thinks will make him so; he seldom attains his goal, and when he does, it is only to be disappointed; he is mostly shipwrecked in the end, and comes into harbor with masts and rigging gone.
quotes.plain: You chase a goal for happiness, reach it, and feel let down.

quotes.text: The scenes of our life are like pictures done in rough mosaic. Looked at close, they produce no effect. There is nothing beautiful to be found in them, unless you stand some distance off.
quotes.plain: Your life only looks good from a distance. Up close it is rough.

quotes.text: We look upon the present as something to be put up with while it lasts, and serving only as the way towards our goal.
quotes.plain: You treat today as a waiting room, and it is the actual life.

quotes.text: Of how many a man may it not be said that hope made a fool of him until he danced into the arms of death!
quotes.plain: Do not spend your whole life waiting on something that never comes.

quotes.text: Every satisfaction he attains lays the seeds of some new desire, so that there is no end to the wishes of each individual will.
quotes.plain: Getting what you want just makes you want more.

quotes.text: The first task is to win something; the second, to banish the feeling that it has been won; otherwise it is a burden.
quotes.plain: First you have to earn it, then you have to keep from going numb.

quotes.text: Human life must be some kind of mistake.
quotes.plain: Sometimes existence itself looks like a mistake.

quotes.text: It is only in the microscope that our life looks so big. It is an indivisible point, drawn out and magnified by the powerful lenses of Time and Space.
quotes.plain: Zoom out and your problems shrink to nothing.

quotes.text: Reason deserves to be called a prophet; for in showing us the consequence and effect of our actions in the present, does it not tell us what the future will be?
quotes.plain: Think through what your action leads to before you do it.

quotes.text: Hatred comes from the heart; contempt from the head; and neither feeling is quite within our control.
quotes.plain: You cannot simply decide to stop feeling hatred or contempt.

quotes.text: Contempt is not incompatible with indulgent and kindly treatment, and for the sake of one's own peace and safety, this should not be omitted; it will prevent irritation; and there is no one who cannot do harm if he is roused to it.
quotes.plain: You can look down on someone and still be polite. It keeps you safe.

quotes.text: Hypochondria shows itself in a perpetual hunting after things that vex and annoy, and then brooding over them.
quotes.plain: Stop hunting for things to be upset about and then chewing on them.

quotes.text: Any incident, however trivial, that rouses disagreeable emotion, leaves an after-effect in our mind, which for the time it lasts, prevents our taking a clear objective view of the things about us, and tinges all our thoughts: just as a small object held close to the eye limits and distorts our field of vision.
quotes.plain: One small annoyance can warp how you see everything. Step back.

quotes.text: What makes people hard-hearted is this, that each man has, or fancies he has, as much as he can bear in his own troubles.
quotes.plain: People are cold because they are carrying their own weight.

quotes.text: In my head there is a permanent opposition-party; and whenever I take any step or come to any decision, though I may have given the matter mature consideration, it afterwards attacks what I have done, without, however, being each time necessarily in the right.
quotes.plain: That voice second-guessing every choice is not always right.

quotes.text: In giving way to emotion of this violent kind, the greatest genius puts himself on a level with the commonest son of earth.
quotes.plain: Lose your temper and you are no better than anyone else.

quotes.text: Every man takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world.
quotes.plain: People think what they can see is all there is.

quotes.text: There is no doubt that many a man owes his good fortune in life solely to the circumstance that he has a pleasant way of smiling, and so wins the heart in his favor.
quotes.plain: A good smile gets people further than they deserve.

quotes.text: With people of only moderate ability, modesty is mere honesty; but with those who possess great talent, it is hypocrisy.
quotes.plain: If you are genuinely good, do not pretend you are not.

quotes.text: A doctor can cure everyone but himself; if he falls ill, he sends for a colleague.
quotes.plain: You are blind about your own case. Ask a friend.

quotes.text: In all that we do, we wish, more or less, to come to the end; we are impatient to finish and glad to be done. But the last scene of all, the general end, is something that, as a rule, we wish as far off as may be.
quotes.plain: We rush through everything except the one thing that ends it all.

quotes.text: Every parting gives a foretaste of death; every coming together again a foretaste of the resurrection.
quotes.plain: Saying goodbye feels like a small death, and reunion feels like coming back to life.

quotes.text: The scenes and events of long ago, and the persons who took part in them, wear a charming aspect to the eye of memory, which sees only the outlines and takes no note of disagreeable details. The present enjoys no such advantage, and so it always seems defective.
quotes.plain: The past looks better than it was, so today always loses the comparison.

quotes.text: It is a curious fact that in bad days we can very vividly recall the good time that is now no more; but that in good days, we have only a very cold and imperfect memory of the bad.
quotes.plain: On bad days you remember the good times. On good days you forget how bad it was.

quotes.text: Men need some kind of external activity, because they are inactive within.
quotes.plain: People who keep busy all the time are often avoiding their own head.

quotes.text: The fatal tendency to be satisfied with words instead of trying to understand things, to learn phrases by heart, so that they may prove a refuge in time of need, exists, as a rule, even in children; and the tendency lasts on into manhood, making the knowledge of many learned persons to consist in mere verbiage.
quotes.plain: Knowing the phrases isn't knowing the thing. Words are a cheap stand-in for understanding.

quotes.text: Childhood and youth form the time for collecting materials, for getting a special and thorough knowledge of the individual and particular things.
quotes.plain: Youth is for gathering raw material. The big conclusions come later.

quotes.text: Maturity is the work of experience alone; and therefore it requires time.
quotes.plain: Real understanding only comes from living it, and that can't be rushed.

quotes.text: If you cut up a large diamond into little bits, it will entirely lose the value it had as a whole; and an army divided up into small bodies of soldiers, loses all its strength.
quotes.plain: Split your attention and you lose most of your power. Focus is the strength.

quotes.text: Noise is the most impertinent of all forms of interruption. It is not only an interruption, but also a disruption of thought.
quotes.plain: Interruptions don't just pause your thinking, they break it.

quotes.text: Hammering, the barking of dogs, and the crying of children are horrible to hear; but your only genuine assassin of thought is the crack of a whip; it exists for the purpose of destroying every pleasant moment of quiet thought that any one may now and then enjoy.
quotes.plain: One sudden loud crack can kill a good thought on the spot.

quotes.text: A man's body and the needs of his body are now everywhere treated with a tender indulgence. Is the thinking mind then, to be the only thing that is never to obtain the slightest measure of consideration or protection, to say nothing of respect?
quotes.plain: We guard the body carefully and treat the thinking mind as disposable. Guard yours.

quotes.text: There are some really beautifully landscapes in the world, but the human figures in them are poor, and you had not better look at them.
quotes.plain: Some things look better from far away.

quotes.text: The fly should be used as the symbol of impertinence and audacity; for whilst all other animals shun man more than anything else, and run away even before he comes near them, the fly lights upon his very nose.
quotes.plain: The pests have no fear of you. Boldness and being impressive are different things.

quotes.text: Wisdom which is only theoretical and never put into practice, is like a double rose; its color and perfume are delightful, but it withers away and leaves no seed.
quotes.plain: Wisdom you never use is just decoration. It dies without producing anything.

quotes.text: No rose without a thorn. Yes, but many a thorn without a rose.
quotes.plain: Pain doesn't guarantee reward. Plenty of hardship comes with no payoff.

quotes.text: As a child, as a youth, often even as a full-grown man, nay, his whole life long, he goes about among his fellows, looking like them and seemingly as unimportant. But let him alone; he will not die. Time will come and bring those who know how to value him.
quotes.plain: Anyone built to last looks ordinary for a long time. Time sorts it out.

quotes.text: The man who goes up in a balloon does not feel as though he were ascending; he only sees the earth sinking deeper under him.
quotes.plain: When you rise, you notice the ground falling away, not yourself climbing.

quotes.text: Your estimation of a man's size will be affected by the distance at which you stand from him, but in two entirely opposite ways according as it is his physical or his mental stature that you are considering. The one will seem smaller, the farther off you move; the other, greater.
quotes.plain: Distance shrinks people of body and magnifies people of mind.

quotes.text: Every hero is a Samson. The strong man succumbs to the intrigues of the weak and the many; and if in the end he loses all patience he crushes both them and himself.
quotes.plain: The strong get worn down by the many small ones, and sometimes break everything.

quotes.text: The moderate distance which they at last discover to be the only tolerable condition of intercourse, is the code of politeness and fine manners; and those who transgress it are roughly told, in the English phrase, to keep their distance.
quotes.plain: Closeness hurts, so politeness is just the right amount of space between people.

quotes.text: A man who has some heat in himself prefers to remain outside, where he will neither prick other people nor get pricked himself.
quotes.plain: If you're warm inside, you don't need to crowd others for warmth.

quotes.text: How shall a man be proud, when his conception is a crime, his birth a penalty, his life a labour, and death a necessity!
quotes.plain: Birth, work and death are not much to be proud of. Stay humble.

quotes.text: Do not consider his bad will, or his narrow understanding and perverse ideas; as the former may easily lead you to hate and the latter to despise him; but fix your attention only upon his sufferings, his needs, his anxieties, his pains.
quotes.plain: Look at what a person is suffering and it's hard to hate them.

quotes.text: The way to keep down hatred and contempt is certainly not to look for a man's alleged "dignity," but, on the contrary, to regard him as an object of pity.
quotes.plain: Don't judge people by their worth. See their pain and the hatred fades.

quotes.text: Envy builds the wall between Thee and Me thicker and stronger; Sympathy makes it slight and transparent; nay, sometimes it pulls down the wall altogether; and then the distinction between self and not-self vanishes.
quotes.plain: Envy makes you feel separate from people. Sympathy takes the wall down.

quotes.text: Courage, however, may also be explained as a readiness to meet ills that threaten at the moment, in order to avoid greater ills that lie in the future; whereas cowardice does the contrary.
quotes.plain: Courage is taking a smaller hit now to avoid a bigger one later.

quotes.text: Extravagance springs from a brutish limitation to the present moment, in comparison with which the future, existing as it does only in thought, is as nothing.
quotes.plain: The spender lives only in the present, and the future costs him nothing until it arrives.

quotes.text: Every human perfection is allied to a defect into which it threatens to pass; but it is also true that every defect is allied to a perfection.
quotes.plain: Every strength has a flaw next to it and every flaw a strength.

quotes.text: The cautious man seems to us a coward; the economical man, a miser; the spendthrift seems liberal; the rude fellow, downright and sincere; the foolhardy person looks as if he were going to work with a noble self-confidence; and so on in many other cases.
quotes.plain: We mistake flaws for virtues in people we've just met. Look closer.

quotes.text: A man who is unintelligent is very likely to show his perfidy, villainy and malice; whereas a clever man understands how to conceal these qualities.
quotes.plain: Fools show their malice openly, clever people hide it.

quotes.text: Just as every man, though he be the greatest genius, has very definite limitations in some one sphere of knowledge, and thus attests his common origin with the essentially perverse and stupid mass of mankind, so also has every man something in his nature which is positively evil.
quotes.plain: Nobody is above flaws, not even the best. No need to hate yourself for yours.

quotes.text: It is very necessary that a man should be apprised early in life that it is a masquerade in which he finds himself.
quotes.plain: Learn early that most people are wearing masks.

quotes.text: Man is at bottom a savage, horrible beast. We know it, if only in the business of taming and restraining him which we call civilisation.
quotes.plain: Civilization is a leash on something wild. Don't forget it's there.

quotes.text: In every man there dwells, first and foremost, a colossal egoism, which breaks the bounds of right and justice with the greatest freedom, as everyday life shows on a small scale, and as history on every page of it on a large.
quotes.plain: Everyone is deeply selfish and will bend rules for it. Plan around that.

quotes.text: That anger is not without its pleasure is a truth that was recorded even by Aristotle; and he quotes a passage from Homer, who declares anger to be sweeter than honey.
quotes.plain: Anger feels good, and that is exactly why it's dangerous.

quotes.text: No animal ever torments another for the mere purpose of tormenting, but man does it, and it is this that constitutes the diabolical feature in his character which is so much worse than the merely animal.
quotes.plain: Only people hurt others purely to hurt them.

quotes.text: Right in itself is powerless; in nature it is Might that rules.
quotes.plain: Being right is not enough. It needs strength behind it.

quotes.text: Everywhere and at all times there has been much discontent with governments, laws and public regulations; for the most part, however, because men are always ready to make institutions responsible for the misery inseparable from human existence itself; which is, to speak mythically, the curse that was laid on Adam, and through him on the whole race.
quotes.plain: People blame governments for the pain that comes with being alive.

quotes.text: Formerly it was faith which was the chief support of the throne; nowadays it is credit.
quotes.plain: What holds power up changes with the age. Now it's trust in money.

quotes.text: It amounts to this, that by what we do we know what we are, and by what we suffer we know what we deserve.
quotes.plain: You learn who you are from what you do, not from what you intend.

quotes.text: The man who has no conscience in small things will be a scoundrel in big things.
quotes.plain: How you act when it's small is how you'll act when it's big.

quotes.text: Let it always be our maxim: Better alone than amongst traitors.
quotes.plain: Cut off bad company early. Being alone beats being betrayed.

quotes.text: No man becomes this or that by wishing to be it, however earnestly.
quotes.plain: Wishing doesn't change who you are. Your actions show it.

quotes.text: Conscience accompanies every act with the comment: You should act differently, although its true sense is: You could be other than you are.
quotes.plain: Guilt is a signal that you can be a different person.

quotes.text: As a man is, so must he act; and praise or blame attaches, not to his separate acts, but to his nature and being.
quotes.plain: You are judged by what you are, not by one act. Work on the person.

quotes.text: Imitation and custom are the spring of almost all human action.
quotes.plain: Most people just copy what's around them. Notice when you're doing it.

quotes.text: Men who aspire to a happy, a brilliant and a long life, instead of to a virtuous one, are like foolish actors who want to be always having the great parts, the parts that are marked by splendour and triumph. They fail to see that the important thing is not what or how much, but how they act.
quotes.plain: Don't chase the starring role. How you play the part is what counts.

quotes.text: Life is the proof sheet, in which the compositors' errors are brought to light.
quotes.plain: Life exposes your mistakes so you can see them and fix them.

quotes.text: Character modifies our life more than we think, and it is to a certain extent true that every man is the architect of his own fortune.
quotes.plain: Who you are shapes your luck more than you admit.

quotes.text: Somebody once remarked to me, with entire justice, that every man had something very good and humane in his disposition, and also something very bad and malignant; and that according as he was moved one or the other of them made its appearance.
quotes.plain: Everyone has a good side and a cruel side. What stirs them decides which shows.

quotes.text: If a man keeps to the exact middle, he is just. But most men go an inch in their regard for others' welfare to twenty yards in regard for their own.
quotes.plain: Almost everyone weighs themselves far heavier than anyone else.

quotes.text: The practical philosopher transforms ideas into life; he acts, therefore, in a thoroughly reasonable manner; he is consistent, regular, deliberate; he is never hasty or passionate; he never allows himself to be influenced by the impression of the moment.
quotes.plain: The one who lives his ideas is steady, deliberate, and not pushed around by the moment.

quotes.text: Innocence is in its very nature stupid.
quotes.plain: Staying untested isn't a virtue. You learn by running into things.

quotes.text: The paltry character of most men compels the few who have any merit or genius to behave as though they did not know their own value, and consequently did not know other people's want of value; for it is only on this condition that the mob acquiesces in tolerating merit.
quotes.plain: Good people play small so the crowd will put up with them.

quotes.text: Insight and knowledge may be attained and lost again; they may be changed, or improved, or destroyed; but will cannot be changed.
quotes.plain: Knowledge comes and goes. Will is who you are, and it doesn't move.

quotes.text: A man should exercise an almost boundless toleration and placability, because if he is capricious enough to refuse to forgive a single individual for the meanness or evil that lies at his door, it is doing the rest of the world a quite unmerited honour.
quotes.plain: Forgive freely. Holding a grudge against one person isn't worth what it costs you.

quotes.text: It is only because the will is above and beyond time that the stings of conscience are ineradicable, and do not, like other pains, gradually wear away. No! an evil deed weighs on the conscience years afterwards as heavily as if it had been freshly committed.
quotes.plain: Guilt doesn't fade with time. Don't do what you'll have to carry.

quotes.text: Many a criminal dies more quietly on the scaffold than many a non-criminal in the arms of his family.
quotes.plain: Facing yourself brings peace. Avoiding yourself doesn't.

quotes.text: Every feeble lad who by little acts of villainy gains a small advantage for himself by putting others to some disadvantage, although it may be equally small, is just as bad as Napoleon.
quotes.plain: Small cruelty is the same thing as big cruelty, just without the power.

quotes.text: No one writes anything that is worth writing, unless he writes entirely for the sake of his subject.
quotes.plain: Do the work for the work. Chasing money ruins the output.

quotes.text: What an inestimable boon it would be, if in every branch of literature there were only a few books, but those excellent!
quotes.plain: Less and better beats more and mediocre.

quotes.text: The best works of the greatest men all come from the time when they had to write for nothing or for very little.
quotes.plain: Great work usually comes before the money does.

quotes.text: Unless an author takes the material on which he writes out of his own head, that is to say, from his own observation, he is not worth reading.
quotes.plain: Say what you've seen yourself, not what you've collected.

quotes.text: How very learned many a man would be if he knew everything that was in his own books!
quotes.plain: Owning information is not knowing it.

quotes.text: And, in general, the following rule may be laid down here as elsewhere: if a thing is new, it is seldom good; because if it is good, it is only for a short time new.
quotes.plain: New is not the same as good. Time sorts it out.

quotes.text: Style is the physiognomy of the mind, and a safer index to character than the face.
quotes.plain: How you write shows who you are.

quotes.text: An affectation in style is like making grimaces.
quotes.plain: Faking a voice looks as silly as pulling faces.

quotes.text: And yet nothing is easier than to write so that no one can understand; just as contrarily, nothing is more difficult than to express deep things in such a way that every one must necessarily grasp them.
quotes.plain: Being confusing is easy. Being clear about hard things is the real skill.

quotes.text: Simplicity has always been held to be a mark of truth; it is also a mark of genius.
quotes.plain: Say it plainly. Plain is how true and brilliant things sound.

quotes.text: Style is nothing but the mere silhouette of thought; and an obscure or bad style means a dull or confused brain.
quotes.plain: Muddy writing is muddy thinking.

quotes.text: The first rule, then, for a good style is that the author should have something to say; nay, this is in itself almost all that is necessary.
quotes.plain: Have something to say. Everything else is secondary.

quotes.text: Authors should use common words to say uncommon things.
quotes.plain: Think big, speak plainly.

quotes.text: When a right thought springs up in the mind, it strives after expression and is not long in reaching it; for clear thought easily finds words to fit it.
quotes.plain: If you can't say it clearly, you haven't finished thinking.

quotes.text: It is always better to omit something good than to add that which is not worth saying at all.
quotes.plain: Cut. Leave out the good if it isn't needed.

quotes.text: To use many words to communicate few thoughts is everywhere the unmistakable sign of mediocrity. To gather much thought into few words stamps the man of genius.
quotes.plain: Few words, lots of thought. Padding is a tell.

quotes.text: Truth is most beautiful undraped; and the impression it makes is deep in proportion as its expression has been simple.
quotes.plain: The simpler you say a true thing, the harder it hits.

quotes.text: Man that is born of a woman hath but a short time to live and is full of misery. He cometh up, and is cut down, like a flower; he fleeth as it were a shadow, and never continueth in one stay.
quotes.plain: Life is short and hard, and plain words say it best.

quotes.text: Every word that can be spared is hurtful if it remains.
quotes.plain: If it can go, cut it.

quotes.text: He who writes carelessly confesses thereby at the very outset that he does not attach much importance to his own thoughts.
quotes.plain: Sloppy work tells people you don't take your own ideas seriously.

quotes.text: There is no better recreation for the mind than the study of the ancient classics. Take any one of them into your hand, be it only for half an hour, and you will feel yourself refreshed, relieved, purified, ennobled, strengthened; just as though you had quenched your thirst at some pure spring.
quotes.plain: Thirty minutes with an old great book resets your head better than rest.

quotes.text: Every thirty years a new race comes into the world, a youngster that knows nothing about anything, and after summarily devouring in all haste the results of human knowledge as they have been accumulated for thousands of years, aspires to be thought cleverer than the whole of the past.
quotes.plain: Every generation thinks it's smarter than all that came before.

quotes.text: Students, and learned persons of all sorts and every age, aim as a rule at acquiring information rather than insight.
quotes.plain: Collecting facts isn't understanding. Aim for insight.

quotes.text: When I hear of these portents of learning and their imposing erudition, I sometimes say to myself: Ah, how little they must have had to think about, to have been able to read so much!
quotes.plain: Reading nonstop can be a way to avoid thinking.

quotes.text: With by far the largest number of learned men, knowledge is a means, not an end.
quotes.plain: Most people use what they know to get something. Few love it for itself.

quotes.text: He alone will be really in earnest about a matter, who has a direct interest therein, takes to it because he likes it, and pursues it con amore. It is these, and not hirelings, that have always done the greatest work.
quotes.plain: The people who do it for love do the greatest work.

quotes.text: The only thing in which all agree is in trying to keep down a really eminent man, if he should chance to show himself, as one who would be a common peril.
quotes.plain: Standouts get pushed down. Expect it.

quotes.text: Human knowledge extends on all sides farther than the eye can reach; and of that which would be generally worth knowing, no one man can possess even the thousandth part.
quotes.plain: No one can know it all. Pick your ground and go deep.

quotes.text: A library may be very large; but if it is in disorder, it is not so useful as one that is small but well arranged.
quotes.plain: Knowing a lot means little if it's a mess. Organize what you know.

quotes.text: Thinking must be kindled, like a fire by a draught; it must be sustained by some interest in the matter in hand.
quotes.plain: Good thinking needs a spark and something you actually care about.

quotes.text: The safest way of having no thoughts of one's own is to take up a book every moment one has nothing else to do.
quotes.plain: Filling every empty minute with input kills your own thinking.

quotes.text: To read another's thoughts is like taking the leavings of a meal to which we have not been invited, or putting on the clothes which some unknown visitor has laid aside.
quotes.plain: Secondhand ideas are leftovers and hand-me-downs. Make your own.

quotes.text: A man should read only when his own thoughts stagnate at their source, which will happen often enough even with the best of minds.
quotes.plain: Read when you run dry, not to avoid thinking.

quotes.text: Truth that has been merely learned is like an artificial limb, a false tooth, a waxen nose; at best, like a nose made out of another's flesh; it adheres to us only because it is put on. But truth acquired by thinking of our own is like a natural limb; it alone really belongs to us.
quotes.plain: What you only memorized sits on you. What you worked out yourself is part of you.

quotes.text: Reading is thinking with some one else's head instead of one's own.
quotes.plain: When you only consume, you are borrowing someone else's brain.

quotes.text: A man can always sit down and read, but not, think.
quotes.plain: Reading is easy to do on command. Real thinking is not.

quotes.text: It is with thoughts as with men; they cannot always be summoned at pleasure; we must wait for them to come.
quotes.plain: You can't force ideas on schedule. Show up and let them arrive.

quotes.text: Not even the greatest mind is capable of thinking for itself at all times.
quotes.plain: Even the best minds have off hours. You are not broken.

quotes.text: Every one who really thinks for himself is so far like a monarch. His position is undelegated and supreme.
quotes.plain: If you think for yourself, you answer to nobody's authority.

quotes.text: The business of the novelist is not to relate great events, but to make small ones interesting.
quotes.plain: Craft is making ordinary things worth looking at.

quotes.text: Human life is short and fleeting, and many millions of individuals share in it, who are swallowed by that monster of oblivion which is waiting for them with ever-open jaws.
quotes.plain: Millions live and vanish. Do something worth being remembered.

quotes.text: The NEWSPAPER, is the second-hand in the clock of history; and it is not only made of baser metal than those which point to the minute and the hour, but it seldom goes right.
quotes.plain: The news is fast, cheap, and usually wrong.

quotes.text: Let us recognize that a newspaper is at best but a magnifying-glass, and very often merely a shadow on the wall.
quotes.plain: News blows things up or makes them up. Don't let it rule your mood.

quotes.text: The pen is to thought what the stick is to walking; but you walk most easily when you have no stick, and you think with the greatest perfection when you have no pen in your hand.
quotes.plain: Your best thinking happens before you grab the tool.

quotes.text: If a man wants to read good books, he must make a point of avoiding bad ones; for life is short, and time and energy limited.
quotes.plain: Time is short. Cut the junk so the good stuff gets your attention.

quotes.text: The source of all pleasure and delight is the feeling of kinship.
quotes.plain: We enjoy what feels like us. Find your people.

quotes.text: There are two ways of behaving in regard to merit: either to have some of one's own, or to refuse any to others. The latter method is more convenient, and so it is generally adopted.
quotes.plain: Building your own worth is hard. Tearing down others is easy, and most people choose easy.

quotes.text: As envy is a mere sign of deficiency, so to envy merit argues the lack of it.
quotes.plain: Envy tells you what the envier lacks. Don't take it personally.

quotes.text: Contrarily, a reputation that is to last a long time must be slow in maturing, and the centuries of its duration have generally to be bought at the cost of contemporary praise.
quotes.plain: Lasting work is paid for by going unpraised for a long time.

quotes.text: Men of great genius, whether their work be in poetry, philosophy or art, stand in all ages like isolated heroes, keeping up single-handed a desperate struggling against the onslaught of an army of opponents.
quotes.plain: Great people always stand nearly alone against the crowd.

quotes.text: When I watch the behavior of a crowd of people in the presence of some great master's work, and mark the manner of their applause, they often remind me of trained monkeys in a show.
quotes.plain: Crowd applause is often imitation, not understanding.

quotes.text: As a rule, people discover a man to be worth listening to only after he is gone; their hear, hear, resounds when the orator has left the platform.
quotes.plain: People applaud after you're gone. Don't wait on it.

quotes.text: Does the worm see the eagle as it soars aloft?
quotes.plain: Small minds can't see high ones. Don't wait for them to understand you.

quotes.text: As it is a rare thing for even one man out of many millions to tread the path that leads to immortality, he must of necessity be very lonely.
quotes.plain: A rare path is a lonely one. That's the price.

quotes.text: Meanwhile let me before all things recommend the traveler to take light baggage with him; otherwise he will have to throw away too much on the road.
quotes.plain: On a long road, carry less or you'll drop it all anyway.

quotes.text: Reverence cannot endure close proximity; it almost always dwells at some distance from its object; and in the presence of the person revered it melts like butter in the sun.
quotes.plain: Admiration fades up close. Nobody is a hero to those who see them daily.

quotes.text: When the facts themselves are eloquent of a truth, there is no need to rush to its aid with words: for time will give it a thousand tongues.
quotes.plain: If you're right, time will argue for you. Stop over-explaining.

quotes.text: As our emblem and coat of arms, I propose a tree mightily shaken by the wind, but still bearing its ruddy fruit on every branch; with the motto Dum convellor mitescunt, or Conquassata sed ferax.
quotes.plain: Get shaken by the storm and keep bearing fruit.

quotes.text: In order to have original, uncommon, and perhaps even immortal thoughts, it is enough to estrange oneself so fully from the world of things for a few moments, that the most ordinary objects and events appear quite new and unfamiliar.
quotes.plain: Original ideas come from seeing the ordinary as if for the first time.

quotes.text: The mind of genius is among other minds what the carbuncle is among precious stones: it sends forth light of its own, while the others reflect only that which they have received.
quotes.plain: Be a source of light, not a mirror.

quotes.text: A man of learning is a man who has learned a great deal; a man of genius, one from whom we learn something which the genius has learned from nobody.
quotes.plain: Don't just collect knowledge. Produce something new.

quotes.text: He who wishes to experience gratitude from his contemporaries, must adjust his pace to theirs. But great things are never produced in this way.
quotes.plain: If you want applause now, you'll make average work. Move at your own pace.

quotes.text: What man has in any real sense lived more than he whose moments of thought make their echoes heard through the tumult of centuries?
quotes.plain: Real living is making something that outlasts you.

quotes.text: Great minds thus owe little ones some indulgence; for it is only in virtue of these little minds that they themselves are great.
quotes.plain: Be patient with smaller people. Greatness is measured against them.

quotes.text: It is often the case that a great mind prefers soliloquy to the dialogue he may have in this world.
quotes.plain: Sometimes your best company is your own head.

quotes.text: Great, genuine and extraordinary work can be done only in so far as its author disregards the method, the thoughts, the opinions of his contemporaries, and quietly works on, in spite of their criticism, on his side despising what they praise.
quotes.plain: Great work needs you to ignore what everyone else thinks and keep going.

quotes.text: To read a philosopher's biography, instead of studying his thoughts, is like neglecting a picture and attending only to the style of its frame, debating whether it is carved well or ill, and how much it cost to gild it.
quotes.plain: Study the work and the ideas, not the gossip around them.

quotes.text: Glory is such an uncertain thing, and, if you look at it closely, of so little value.
quotes.plain: Fame is flimsy. Don't build your life on it.

quotes.text: Hardly one in ten thousand will have the strength of mind to ask himself seriously and earnestly, is that true?
quotes.plain: Almost nobody asks whether what they believe is true. Be the one who does.

quotes.text: The flag to which I have taken the oath is truth; I shall remain faithful to it everywhere, and whether I succeed or not, I shall fight for light and truth!
quotes.plain: Pick truth as your flag and stay loyal whether you win or lose.

quotes.text: The truth, my dear sir, is the only safe thing; the truth alone remains steadfast and trusty; it is the only solid consolation; it is the indestructible diamond.
quotes.plain: Only truth holds up under pressure.

quotes.text: To free a man from error is to give, not to take away. Knowledge that a thing is false is a truth.
